intro: Many phrasal verbs (turn off, pick up, fill in…) allow their object to go in the middle: “turn the light off” or “turn off the light”. But with a pronoun there is no choice: “turn it off”. Mastering this word-order rule removes a very noticeable mistake.
objectifs: Tell the difference between separable, inseparable and intransitive phrasal verbs.
Place a noun object (two possible positions) and a pronoun object (only one position) correctly.
Know about twenty very common separable phrasal verbs and their meanings.
Use a dictionary to check whether a phrasal verb is separable.

texte: A phrasal verb combines a verb and a particle (up, off, on, out, down, back, away…). The meaning is often different from the verb alone: “give up” means “stop trying”, which has nothing to do with giving.

For word order, there are three families. Intransitive verbs have no object: get up, break down, grow up. Separable verbs allow the object between the verb and the particle. Inseparable verbs always have the object after the particle.

lignes: get up, break down, go out, grow up, set off
no object: The car broke down.
turn off, pick up, fill in, put on, throw away
turn off the TV / turn the TV off / turn it off
look after, get on (a bus), run into, come across, look for
look after the kids / look after them (never “look them after”)

sections.titre: The golden rule: pronouns go in the middle
texte: With a separable verb and a NOUN object, both positions are correct: “Can you pick up the kids?” = “Can you pick the kids up?”.

With a PRONOUN object (it, them, him, her, me, us, you), the pronoun must go between the verb and the particle: “pick them up”, never “pick up them”. This is the most frequent mistake with phrasal verbs.

lignes: Put on your coat. / Put your coat on.
I threw away the old shoes. / I threw the old shoes away.

exemples: Turn the music down, please. — OK, I'll turn it down.
Noun in the middle, then pronoun in the middle.
Could you fill in this form? — Sure, I'll fill it in now.
Noun after the particle, pronoun in the middle.

texte: When the object is long (a noun with a lot of information, or a clause), put it after the particle. Putting it in the middle makes the sentence hard to follow, because the listener waits too long for the particle.
In practice: short object → both positions; long object → after the particle; pronoun → in the middle.
exemples: Please pick up the documents that I left on the reception desk.
We need to sort out the problem with the delivery to our client in Kinshasa.
She turned down the job offer from the bank in Abidjan.

texte: These verbs are very common in speech and writing. Many have a more formal equivalent of Latin origin: it helps you understand the meaning and choose the register (everyday English clearly prefers the phrasal verb).

lignes: Take them off at the door.
start / stop a machine or light
They offered me a job, but I turned it down.
lift from a surface; collect someone
I'll pick you up at six.
Can you give it back tomorrow?
I don't know this word. I'll look it up.
Write it down so you don't forget.
put on clothes to check them
Let's put it off until Friday.
start talking about; raise a child
Don't bring it up at dinner.
Don't worry, I'll sort it out.

sections.titre: How do you know if a verb is separable?
texte: There is no simple rule. The dictionary tells you: in the Cambridge Dictionary, “turn something off” (with something in the middle) shows a separable verb; “look after someone” (with someone at the end) shows an inseparable verb.
The same verb can change family with its meaning: “take off” (remove clothes) is separable (take it off), but “take off” (a plane leaving the ground) has no object (The plane took off at 9).
exemples: Our plane took off two hours late.
I ran into Fatima at the market.

formule: verb + particle + noun · verb + noun + particle · verb + PRONOUN + particle (turn it off)
prononciation: In a phrasal verb, the main stress usually falls on the particle: turn OFF, pick UP, give BACK.
When a pronoun is in the middle, it is weak and the stress stays on the particle: turn it OFF /ˌtɜːn ɪt ˈɒf/.
Consonant + vowel linking is natural: pick it up /ˌpɪk ɪ ˈtʌp/, turn it off /ˌtɜː nɪ ˈtɒf/.
When a noun follows the phrasal verb, the stress often moves to the noun: turn off the LIGHT.
erreurs: Turn off it.
Turn it off.
Pronoun object: always between the verb and the particle.
I'll pick up you at eight.
I'll pick you up at eight.
The same rule with you, me, him, her, us, them.
Can you look the children after?
Can you look after the children?
look after is inseparable.
She turned the job offer from the international bank down.
She turned down the job offer from the international bank.
Long object: after the particle.
Please fill this form.
Please fill in this form. (US: fill out)
fill alone = make full (a glass); a form: fill in / out.
I'll call back you later.
I'll call you back later.
Pronoun in the middle.
We postponed it off.
We put it off. / We postponed it.
Don't mix the formal verb and the particle.

dialogue.contexte: Saturday morning in a flat in Brussels. Thomas and his flatmate Aminata are tidying up before their friends arrive.
lignes: Can you turn the music down? I can't hear myself think.
Sorry, I'll turn it down. What should I do with these old magazines?
Throw them away. And put your shoes away too, please.
throw them away; put your shoes away.
OK. Oh, your mum called. She asked you to call her back.
I'll call her back later. Did you pick up the cake?
Not yet. I'll pick it up at eleven. The baker wanted to put it off until noon, but I said no.
pick it up; put it off = postpone.
Good. And I've set up the speaker on the balcony.
Great — but don't turn it up too much. The neighbours will complain!
turn it up = make it louder.

mots: “Give up” is a common phrasal verb.
a verb + particle with a special meaning
a small word like up, off, out in a phrasal verb
an official paper with spaces for information
to move an event to a later time (formal for put off)
a button that turns electricity on or off
things you throw away (US: garbage, trash)
a proposal to give someone something, e.g. a job
The object goes between the verb and the particle.
the person or thing that a verb acts on
a word like it, them, her used instead of a noun
Our neighbours complained about the noise.
a person who lives near you (US: neighbor)

exercices.consigne: Describe a busy day (tidying, moving house, work) in five or six sentences with at least six phrasal verbs, three of them with a pronoun.
items: Model answer

Last Saturday we moved to a new flat in Lyon. In the morning I picked up the van and my friends helped me. We took the old furniture apart and threw most of it away. My sister found some old letters, but I didn't want to throw them away, so I put them away in a box. In the evening I set up the internet, but it didn't work, so I called the company and they sorted it out.

a_retenir: Separable verb + noun: two positions (turn off the TV / turn the TV off).
Separable verb + pronoun: always in the middle (turn it off, pick them up).
Inseparable verbs (look after, run into, come across): object always after the particle.
The dictionary shows the position: turn something off (separable) / look after someone (inseparable).
